source.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
source.authors: Jia-Chuan Wang; Shimin Di; Lei Chen; Charles Wang Wai Ng

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies neuron monosemanticity and interventions intended to reduce it, but does not test overlapping feature directions, capacity competition, or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports the paper's own Pythia-v0 neuron-deactivation experiment, so it is recorded as a related finding under none rather than assigned to a claim version: it measures loss changes, not superposition geometry or capacity pressure. Tables 1–5 report task performance or validate the paper's induced inhibition method; they do not test the claim versions. Claims about sparse features and importance, and references to SAE features, are not tested.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an online monosemanticity score and a training-time inhibition module (MEmeL), and reports task performance. It does not measure feature geometry, capacity competition, dictionary or SAE features, or feature dimensionality. The Figure 2 Pythia neuron-deactivation result is a motivating loss measure on one probe-selected neuron per model. It cannot show whether features are superposed or spread across neurons. Table 4 measures monosemanticity changes the method induces on purpose, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors hypothesize that fewer monosemantic neurons drive gains with scale. They report that MEmeL (reverse deactivation) reduces their monosemanticity score and gives small fine-tuning gains on GLUE, ImageNet and HKO-7. The paired t-tests give p of 0.02 to 0.07, and the authors call these significant at 90% confidence. Tests on LLM-scale models are left as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it proposes a neuron-level metric and an inhibition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Figure 2 reports a smaller loss increase from deactivating a French-associated neuron at larger tested Pythia-v0 sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a probe-selected French neuron in Pythia-v0 raises loss mainly on French inputs. The increase is smaller at larger sizes (70M, 1B, 6.9B), figure only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss impact of ablating a single feature-selective neuron declines with model scale.

record.problems: The claim-relevant adjacent Pythia result is shown only in a figure, without numerical values or stated uncertainty. The paper says its work could not be extended to very large models such as LLMs.

untested.parts: All: toy models, sparsity transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition and importance-based allocation.
All: distributed features in LLMs and SAE recovery. Figure 2 is a single-neuron ablation loss, not a distribution measure.
All: SAE feature completeness, stability and canonicity.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not cite Toy Models of Superposition. It relies on Elhage et al. (SoLU), Gurnee et al. (sparse probing) and Bricken et al. (dictionary learning) only as background. The Table 4 monosemanticity decrease ratios (e.g. 0.013% for reverse deactivation) describe the method's own induced effect, so no rows are needed. The scale trend in Figure 2 rests on one neuron per model and gives no numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, excess sparse features, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, and sparsity-dependent geometric transitions.
Whether limited capacity causes feature competition, or important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise by mechanisms other than capacity pressure, and whether they evidence superposition.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons or sparse features are recovered by a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical representation units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relation.reason: The paper discusses monosemanticity, polysemanticity and distributed representations without testing feature superposition, capacity competition or dictionary features.

tranche.reason: The study measures selected neurons' ablation effects and evaluates monosemanticity inhibition. These results do not test any listed claim version or use superposition as a tool.

source_check.notes: Figure 2 reports loss increase in percent, with no numerical results stated in the extracted text. Its selected-neuron ablations establish feature-specific importance, not feature distribution across neurons.
